rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient at mid temperature to observe the full elution window and avoid missing retained compounds. This should reveal whether peaks are unretained, elute during the gradient, or require stronger/longer conditions, guiding later window and slope optimization.

Only one critical pair is failing, and all compounds already elute by 9.4 min, so the next informative move is to halve the gradient steepness while keeping the same phi window and temperature. This tests whether the 4/5 pair is slope-responsive; if R improves strongly, we can later shorten or trim the window around that condition.

The broad runs show all peaks elute in a narrow effective solvent window around mid-gradient, so trimming the gradient to that window should preserve selectivity while greatly reducing run time. With the critical pair clearly slope-responsive, a 10 min gradient over a narrower phi range is a good first attempt to keep it resolved while staying under the 10 min time limit.

The narrowed window was effective for speed but too steep, creating several under-resolved pairs. Doubling tG at the same trimmed window directly tests whether those pairs, especially 4/5, can be resolved while likely keeping t_last still below 10 min.

Changing the phi window compressed selectivity and made new coelutions, so the original broad gradient is the better base. Since the 4/5 pair was strongly slope-responsive in the broad window yet full resolution at 40 min was too slow, the next lever is temperature: lowering T may shift selectivity enough to open the critical pair while keeping t_last under 10 min.

At 25 C the broad window is almost ideal: only one pair is slightly below 1.5 and the time penalty is small. A modest shortening of tG should pull t_last under 10 min and may keep the critical pair near the resolution threshold, probing whether this condition can reach a higher CRF by trading a little resolution for time.

The 3/4 pair is very sensitive to gradient steepness at 25 C: shortening to 18 min dropped it well below threshold, while 20 min was close. A small increase to 22 min should push that pair to full credit, and the slight time penalty is likely smaller than the resolution gain.

At 25 C and 20 min only one pair is just below threshold, so a small temperature increase is the best next selectivity probe. This may keep the improved 3/4 spacing while shaving enough retention to remove the slight time penalty and improve CRF over the current best.

The best condition is still 20 min at 25 C, and all peaks elute well before the programmed gradient ends, so the upper end of the window is wider than needed. Lowering phi1 slightly should shallow the gradient around the active elution region and may nudge the borderline pair above 1.5, while only modestly increasing retention.

A 5 C increase to 30 C worsened selectivity by creating a severe early coelution, so the next unused temperature probe is 35 C to map that trend more completely and confirm the optimum lies on the low-temperature side. This gives more information on temperature-driven order/selectivity changes without repeating prior slope or window settings.

At 25 C, lowering phi1 from 0.95 to 0.90 fully resolved all pairs but cost too much time; the next logical move is to narrow the window a bit more from the top while staying at the best temperature. This tests whether selectivity remains fully resolved and whether the stronger late retention hurts or helps overall CRF relative to the current best.

The strongest remaining uncertainty is whether a larger temperature shift can create a different selectivity regime, since moderate increases caused pair switching and new coelutions. A high-temperature scout on the proven broad gradient will quickly map that alternative selectivity space while keeping all compounds eluting within the time window.

At 60 C the run is comfortably under 10 min and only one pair is slightly below 1.5, so a small increase in tG is the cleanest way to improve that pair without risking a time penalty. This should test whether full or near-full resolution can be reached while still keeping t_last below 10 min.

At 60 C the critical 5/6 pair became much worse when the gradient was lengthened, so it responds opposite to the earlier 25 C case. Shortening tG should therefore improve that pair further while also keeping the run comfortably short, offering the best chance to exceed the current best CRF.

The current best is extremely close to ideal, with only one pair just under the 1.5 threshold and plenty of spare time margin. A further 2 min reduction tests whether the critical pair can be nudged over 1.5 in this selectivity regime while retaining a very short run, which could achieve the maximum CRF.

18 min at 60 C is nearly optimal, and all peaks elute well before the end of the gradient, so a slight reduction in phi1 is the best fine-tuning move. This should modestly reshape selectivity in the active elution region and may push the lone borderline pair over 1.5 while retaining a comfortable sub-10 min t_last.

The 18 min broad gradient is clearly the right shape, and the remaining issue is a single near-threshold pair whose identity shifts with selectivity changes. A 5 C step down from 60 C is the cleanest fine-tuning move to see if that pair opens slightly without sacrificing the short run, potentially converting the near-perfect method into a fully resolved one.

The best method has the first peak still fairly early, so raising phi0 one step is a sensible fine adjustment that slightly narrows the effective gradient window without changing its end or duration. This may redistribute selectivity among the crowded middle peaks and push the lone borderline pair over 1.5 while keeping the run short.

We have mapped 55 and 60 C at the best gradient and seen a sharp selectivity change, so 50 C is the remaining untested temperature in that local region. This checks for a narrow temperature optimum that might fully resolve the borderline pair while preserving the short run seen near 60 C.

The selectivity transition between 40 and 60 C is clearly non-monotonic, so 45 C is worth testing as the last missing temperature on the best 18 min broad gradient. It is unlikely to beat 60 C, but it is the most informative remaining local probe for any narrow optimum before using the final injections for small window adjustments around the current best.

With the optimum clearly centered at 18 min and 60 C, the last useful lever is the phi window. Lowering phi1 another step from 0.90 tests whether a slightly shallower high-temperature gradient can convert the remaining near-threshold pair to full resolution while still keeping t_last safely under 10 min.

We have tested independent one-step changes to phi0 and phi1 around the best method, and both remained close to optimal but shifted the limiting pair. Combining those two window trims is the most logical remaining fine-tuning experiment and could rebalance the crowded middle region enough to push all adjacent pairs over 1.5 while keeping the run very short.

The current best is only 0.01 resolution units short of full credit on one pair, and there is ample time margin. A small increase in tG at the same optimized window and temperature is the most direct way to try to push that lone pair over 1.5 and reach the maximum CRF.

At the current best condition only one pair is 0.01 below full credit, and raising phi0 previously shifted congestion earlier without hurting run time. A further one-step increase in phi0 at the same phi1, tG, and temperature is the most promising remaining fine-tune to rebalance the crowded middle pair and possibly cross the 1.5 threshold.

The best condition is 0.10–0.90, 18 min, 60 C with only one pair at R 1.49; increasing tG or phi0 alone made things worse, while lowering phi1 alone shifted the bottleneck but stayed close. The last sensible shot is to keep the successful higher phi0 and lower phi1 together, slightly narrowing the window further to see if that tiny remaining deficit can be converted into full resolution without sacrificing the short run.
